body.heading: Poles, and the field between them
paragraphs: Every magnet has two poles, called north and south, where its magnetism is strongest. The rules between poles are simple and absolute: like poles repel, unlike poles attract. Bring two north poles together and they push apart; turn one magnet around and the pair snaps together instead.

Around every magnet stretches an invisible magnetic field — the region where its influence can be felt. Iron filings sprinkled on paper above a bar magnet reveal its shape, lining up in curved strands that leave one pole and enter the other. Cut a magnet in half hoping to isolate a pole and you simply get two smaller magnets, each with both poles.

body.heading: The planet-sized magnet
paragraphs: Earth itself behaves like a giant bar magnet. Deep inside, currents of liquid iron swirling in the outer core generate a planetary magnetic field — a dynamo effect. The field emerges near the south, loops far into space, and re-enters near the north, enveloping the whole planet.

The field is surprisingly feeble at the surface — an ordinary fridge magnet is dozens of times stronger than Earth's field where you stand. Yet it is strong enough to matter enormously: it deflects the solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun that would otherwise strip away the atmosphere over geological time.

body.heading: Where the field touches daily life
paragraphs: Where the field lines dive toward the poles, charged particles funnelled from space collide with the upper atmosphere and light it up: the auroras, the northern and southern lights. The same field turns every compass needle on Earth and guides some migrating animals, which appear to sense it directly.

The field is not fixed. It wobbles measurably within a human lifetime, and the rock record shows it has flipped completely — north becoming south — hundreds of times in Earth's history, most recently about 780,000 years ago. The planet's magnet is a living, restless thing.

description: Like poles repel, unlike attract — and the same magnetism runs a planet-sized dynamo that shields Earth and lights the auroras.
